standouts.title: Investors Are Turning Against Data Centers (Here's Why)
standouts.summary: Scott Galloway and Ed Elson break down why the AI data-center buildout — once Wall Street's safest growth story — is now drawing open skepticism, then cover Netflix's rough year and Oura's upcoming IPO.
args: The capex math is breaking: hyperscalers have issued $132B in debt this year alone while token prices keep collapsing — "the price of AI is collapsing, while the cost of building it is not."

The backlash went political and financial at once: data centers became a midterm-election talking point, and IPOs are stalling — SoftBank's SB Energy pushed its $50B-targeted IPO past mid-October despite Nvidia/OpenAI backing and zero data centers in operation.

Smart money is already pricing the hangover: Michael Burry warned on Sep 24 that write-offs could land around 2028–29; Druckenmiller is concerned about the investment cycle, not the technology itself.
standouts.why: This is the macro fluency that makes you dangerous in client conversations — and it connects straight to the 09-26 All-In thread on the open-source cost squeeze. Your pitch should lean into it: lean, phased AI pilots with measurable returns, not capex-scale commitments. Question to explore, not advice: how do you advise a mid-size client on AI vendor pricing and spend timing when the infra economics underneath are wobbling? Content idea: a LinkedIn post on "what fraction of your AI spend is truly frontier" — the token-price collapse means most enterprise buyers are overpaying.

standouts.show: The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett
standouts.title: Adam Neumann: The Real Story Behind WeWork, A $4 Billion Cab Ride, And Surviving A $460 Million Debt
standouts.summary: Neumann's first long-form interview on the WeWork collapse — from a $47B valuation and 13,000 employees down to three in a week — framed as a founder-psychology conversation rather than a fraud narrative.
args: The ego trap: a 16-minute cab ride in December 2016 where Masayoshi Son overrode his own team and offered $4.2B on an iPad was, by Neumann's account, the moment the mission died — "I forgot what we were all about, and when I lost it, everybody lost it."
Collapse as resilience mechanism: traumatic childhood experiences and the public failure are presented not as curses but as the exact training required to build unbreakable psychological resilience.
Partner selection is the whole game: judge investors, friends, and partners solely by how they treat you on your worst day — and lead by influence from the bottom up, not control from the top.
The Ben Horowitz letter: when everything fell apart, a16z's Horowitz sent a personal note — a reminder that reputation capital is built when you have nothing to offer anyone.
standouts.why: Three direct hits for an Alpha Infra founder: judge prospective clients by worst-day behavior (client selection is partnership selection), influence-over-control as a consulting posture, and the personal-CRM lesson — the relationships you tend when there's no upside are the ones that survive a collapse. Plus a cautionary one on scaling: build foundations before the money arrives, not after. Content idea: "I judge my consulting clients the way Neumann judges his partners" — a strong LinkedIn frame if you want it.
